content: 1. A safe healthcare environment that supports effective infection prevention and control (IPC) practices requires appropriate infrastructure, including the healthcare facility building and the availability of safe water and sanitation facilities, in accordance with international and national standards. 2. Without such infrastructure, IPC measures cannot be effectively implemented, placing healthcare workers, patients, and visitors at significant risk. 3. IPC teams must be involved in the design, construction, and commissioning of new or upgraded healthcare buildings from the earliest stages to ensure safety and compliance with IPC standards. 4. IPC teams should also be engaged during major renovation or demolition projects, as these activities can release large amounts of airborne fungi, posing a serious risk to patient safety. 5. Healthcare facilities must ensure an adequate and continuous supply of safe water, ranging from 5 to 400 liters per person per day, depending on the type of service (e.g., outpatient services require less water, while operating and delivery rooms require more). 6. Safe water must be available in all treatment wards, waiting areas, and for drinking, handwashing, food preparation, personal hygiene, medical activities, cleaning, and laundry, in compliance with WHO guidelines. 7. Water for bathing is essential for pre-surgical preparation, general hygiene, and maintaining the dignity and respect of patients. 8. Water-associated infectious risks, such as Legionellosis, must be appropriately managed to prevent outbreaks. 9. Adequate sanitary facilities must be provided in all healthcare settings, with at least one toilet for every 20 users in inpatient settings, and these facilities must be designed to safely manage excreta. 10. Sanitation facilities should be safe, clean, and accessible to all users, including those with reduced mobility, and should include reliable water points with soap near treatment areas, waiting rooms, and toilets for handwashing. 11. Dedicated clean storage areas for patient care items, sterile materials, and clean linen must be provided, along with separate areas for healthcare waste disposal and sharps management. 12. Risk assessment systems and protective measures must be in place to safeguard patients, families, and staff during construction or renovation, particularly in high-risk areas such as transplant units, intensive care units, neonatal units, burn units, and operating rooms. 13. Negative pressure ventilation may be required in isolation rooms to prevent the transmission of infections, such as multidrug-resistant tuberculosis. 14. If isolation rooms are insufficient, patients with the same infection or multidrug-resistant organism may share a bay, based on IPC team risk assessment. 15. Healthcare facilities must adhere to WHO standards for bed occupancy, ensuring one patient per bed with adequate spacing (at least 1 meter between beds) to prevent cross-contamination. 16. Personal protective equipment (PPE), including non-sterile and sterile gloves, surgical masks, goggles or face shields, gowns, respirators, and aprons, must be available in sufficient quantities and stored in clean, dry areas to prevent contamination. 17. PPE should be single-use whenever possible, and reusable items must have clear policies and procedures for decontamination. 18. Healthcare facilities must implement standardized operating procedures for the safe and effective decontamination of high-touch patient care areas and reusable equipment to prevent cross-infection. 19. Facilities must have dedicated areas for decontamination and sterilization of reusable items, with sufficient and reliable energy to power sterilization devices. 20. Staff working in decontamination units and sterile services departments must receive adequate training and regular updates to ensure compliance with international standards. 21. Isolation involves creating a barrier to prevent the spread of infectious diseases and multidrug-resistant organisms, requiring designated single rooms with private toilet and shower facilities for suspected or confirmed infectious patients. 22. Patients in isolation should be informed about their infection and educated on how to prevent its spread to others. 23. Items used by isolated patients must not be shared between patients, and PPE must be changed after direct contact with each patient, even within the same isolation area. 24. Hand hygiene must be performed at all times, following WHO recommendations and the 5 Moments for Hand Hygiene approach. 25. Patient transport and movement to other wards or departments should be restricted unless medically necessary. 26. For children in isolation, only plastic toys should be allowed, as they can be cleaned and disinfected after use. 27. Visitors to isolation areas should be restricted and informed about the risks of infection, with an emphasis on hand hygiene and the use of appropriate PPE. 28. Healthcare waste management must follow established environmental standards, including waste segregation, collection, transportation, treatment, and final disposal, to prevent infection risks to patients, staff, and the community. 29. Facilities must procure and use single-use devices and safety-engineered injection devices to avoid unsafe practices, such as the reuse of medical devices. 30. Cleaning of healthcare environments must involve the removal of dust, soil, and contaminants to ensure a hygienic and healthy environment for patients, staff, and visitors. 31. Cleaning must precede disinfection to remove debris that can reduce the effectiveness of disinfectants, and neutral detergent solutions should be used for effective cleaning. 32. Special attention should be given to heavily contaminated areas, such as toilets, which are reservoirs for healthcare-associated infections (HAIs). 33. Large-surface cleaning methods that produce mists, aerosols, or disperse dust should be avoided, as airborne fungal spores can cause fatal infections in immunosuppressed patients. 34. Materials and equipment for hand hygiene must be readily available at the point of care to increase compliance with good practices and reduce HAIs, as supported by evidence from multiple studies. 35. The availability and optimal placement of hand hygiene materials and equipment in patient care areas significantly improve hand hygiene compliance. 36. Although the evidence quality is very low, the recommendation for readily available hand hygiene materials and equipment is strong, as it aligns with other key WHO guidelines already implemented worldwide.
